content: Q fever is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Coxiella burnetii. This organism is relatively uncommon but can be found in domestic mammals such as cattle, sheep, goats, cats, and dogs. Humans typically acquire the infection through inhalation of contaminated airborne particles or through contact with the vaginal mucus, milk, feces, urine, or semen of infected animals. The incubation period for Q fever ranges from 9 to 40 days. Remarkably, it is considered one of the most infectious diseases globally, as a single bacterium is sufficient to cause infection in humans. The disease was first described by Edward Holbrook Derrick in Australia, and the causative pathogen was identified in 1937 by Frank Macfarlane Burnet. Q fever can be classified into two forms based on the onset of symptoms: acute and chronic. The causative agent, Coxiella burnetii, is an intracellular, gram-negative proteobacterium. The disease exhibits a wide spectrum of clinical presentations and can affect multiple organ systems due to the unique virulence factors of the organism. The primary reservoirs of Coxiella burnetii include domestic animals such as cattle, sheep, goats, birds, and cats. Some wild animals and ticks also harbor the bacterium. Humans may contract Q fever by consuming raw (unpasteurized) milk or by inhaling dust or droplets contaminated with animal feces, blood, or birth products. Q fever must be differentiated from other diseases that cause atypical pneumonia, such as Mycoplasma pneumonia and legionellosis. The bacterium Coxiella burnetii is found worldwide, except in Antarctica and New Zealand. The disease is slightly more prevalent in elderly individuals and in males. The organism is primarily present in the secretions of cattle and sheep. Occupations involving close contact with these animals, such as farming or veterinary work, increase the risk of contracting the disease. Acute Q fever generally has a favorable prognosis, even without treatment. However, chronic Q fever has a less favorable prognosis and is more challenging to manage. Acute Q fever typically presents with flu-like symptoms, pneumonia, and hepatitis. Chronic Q fever almost always manifests as endocarditis and may occasionally involve musculoskeletal or vascular complications. Patients with Q fever often appear unwell. Physical examination findings commonly include fever, pneumonia, and hepatomegaly. Laboratory findings consistent with Q fever include positive serology for antibodies (especially via indirect immunofluorescence), positive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) results, and elevated liver enzyme levels. On chest X-ray, Q fever may present with signs of atypical pneumonia, such as hazy, non-localized airspace opacities. In some cases, it may show features of typical pneumonia, including lobar consolidation and occasional pleural effusions. Chest CT scans can aid in the diagnosis of Q fever. Findings suggestive of the disease include scattered consolidation and opacities or lobar consolidation in a specific lobe. There are no additional findings on MRI associated with Q fever. Chest X-ray and CT are usually sufficient for diagnosis. Similarly, there are no other specific imaging findings or additional diagnostic studies for Q fever. The primary treatment for Q fever is doxycycline. Chronic Q fever is more difficult to treat and may require up to two years of therapy with a combination of doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine. Treating Q fever during pregnancy is particularly challenging, as doxycycline is contraindicated. In such cases, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole is the preferred treatment. Surgical intervention is not recommended for the management of Q fever. Primary prevention of Q fever involves educating the public about sources of infection, proper disposal of placentas, birth products, fetal membranes, and aborted fetuses at facilities housing sheep and goats, and restricting access to barns and laboratories where potentially infected animals are housed. There are no secondary preventive measures available for Q fever.
